events.title: .NET 3.5 and C# 3.0 with LINQ released
events.summary: Microsoft shipped .NET Framework 3.5 on November 19, 2007 with C# 3.0 LINQ, lambda expressions, and extension methods.
events.about: LINQ let C# developers query databases, XML, and in-memory collections with the same syntax: `from x in list where x.Age > 18 select x.Name`. It changed how .NET teams wrote data access — influencing Entity Framework, ORMs, and reactive patterns for a decade.

narrative.whyChosen: LINQ was the defining language feature of the C# 3 era.
narrative.whyImportant: Unified query syntax across SQL, objects, and XML was a paradigm shift for .NET.
narrative.problemSolved: C# lacked expressive, composable data queries without verbose loops or stringly-typed SQL.

events.title: CouchDB 0.7.0 released
events.summary: Damien Katz released CouchDB 0.7.0 on November 16, 2007 — the first version intended for widespread use with a JSON REST API.
events.about: CouchDB stores documents as JSON with MapReduce views and multi-master replication — offline-first mobile sync (via PouchDB) and eventual consistency without a rigid schema. Example: a field worker saves `{_id: 'job-42', status: 'done'}` offline; CouchDB syncs when connectivity returns.

narrative.whyChosen: CouchDB 0.7.0 stabilized the JSON REST API that defined document-database ergonomics.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved document stores with HTTP interfaces and replication could work in production.
narrative.problemSolved: Relational schemas were awkward for evolving JSON documents and offline mobile sync.

events.title: Android announced
events.summary: Google and the Open Handset Alliance announced Android on November 5, 2007 — an open mobile operating system built on the Linux kernel.
events.about: Android brought Java/Kotlin apps, Google Play distribution, and OEM fragmentation to billions of phones. Developers learned Activities, Gradle builds, and Material Design; mobile web gave way to native Android SDKs alongside iOS. It became the world's dominant smartphone OS within a few years of the first G1.

narrative.whyChosen: Android's announcement defined the open alternative to Apple's closed iPhone platform.
narrative.whyImportant: It created the second major mobile app ecosystem and shaped how most of the world accesses the internet.
narrative.problemSolved: Carriers and handset makers lacked a modern, open smartphone OS to compete with the iPhone.

events.title: OLPC XO-1 laptop released
events.summary: The One Laptop Per Child project began shipping XO-1 laptops in November 2007 — a low-cost, rugged notebook for education in developing countries.
events.about: The XO-1 ran Sugar on Linux with a dual-mode display readable in sunlight — designed for mesh networking and classroom use. Developers contributed to open firmware, Sugar activities, and the Bitfrost security model. Though the million-laptop vision scaled back, OLPC influenced netbooks, ARM education boards, and the Raspberry Pi mission.

narrative.whyChosen: The XO-1 was the flagship $100-laptop project that pushed low-cost computing for education.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved rugged, low-power laptops could be designed for mass deployment outside Western markets.
narrative.problemSolved: Millions of children lacked access to computers for learning programming and digital literacy.
